$comment: Parity policy for the shared VfTextarea cases. Plain data: no DSL, no waiver engine. Every dimension is classified, and every tolerated difference is listed individually with a reason, the exact cases it covers, the exact element it applies to and the number of occurrences it is allowed to have. A difference that is not listed here fails the gate.

classifications.exact: Must match literally across every target. Structure, canonical classes, native attributes, visible text, accessible names, computed geometry and colour.
classifications.semantic: Framework mechanics may differ; the observable meaning must not. Generated id values, how content is composed, how state is stored.
classifications.framework-specific: Historical behaviour of one adapter that the other is not required to reproduce. Narrow, named, and covered by its own test.

notCompared.$comment: Recorded so a reviewer can see what is deliberately outside the comparison, without leaving dead dimensions that look like live protection. Nothing here is a waiver: the extractor never produces these differences in the first place.
notCompared.attributeOrder: Attributes are extracted into a sorted map, so serialisation order cannot produce a difference. It carries no meaning.
notCompared.rendererMarkers: Vue scope attributes (data-v-*) and the Razor ownership marker (data-vf-razor*) are dropped by scripts/parity/extract.mjs. They identify the renderer, not the product. Any other data-* attribute is compared as dom.productData.
notCompared.textareaValueAttribute: HTML defines no value content attribute for textarea. Vue writes one on the client as a side effect of binding :value; a server-rendered control cannot and must not. Comparing it would compare a framework artifact rather than the product, so the extractor drops it for this element type and the compared live value carries the value instead.
notCompared.textareaElementText: A textarea element text is its default value, not content the browser renders - what a user reads is the live value. Vue leaves the text empty and sets the property; Razor writes the text, which is the only form that survives without a client. The extractor drops the text for this element type and compares the live value, which is strictly more than was compared before M13, when nothing described a textarea value at all. Proved by tampering with a rendered value: the comparison still fails.

dom.structure.description: An unexpected element, invalid wrapper arrangement, or tag mismatch. Never approvable; comparison continues through tag differences so meaningful attribute/child diagnostics remain visible.

dom.canonicalClasses.description: vf-* classes on every element. Consumer classes included.

dimensions.dom.nativeAttributes: rows, placeholder, name, maxlength, minlength, spellcheck, autocomplete, wrap, disabled, readonly, required, aria-invalid, aria-label and the style attribute, plus the control live value - the value the element currently holds, read from the element rather than from markup. That live value is the only thing describing a textarea value at all: neither adapter keeps it in a compared attribute, and until M13 nothing recorded it for this element type. scripts/ci/attribute-coverage.test.mjs proves each attribute the profile declares is actually reachable by a comparison.

dom.text.description: Visible text content of every element. See the approved divergence: a textarea is the one element whose text is a value rather than content, and the two adapters transport it differently.

dom.aria.description: role, aria-label, aria-describedby, aria-invalid and aria-hidden. The required marker must be aria-hidden on both adapters so the asterisk is not announced.

dom.productData.description: data-vf-* attributes that carry product semantics, such as data-vf-filled.

dom.actionPresence.description: Whether the button exists and whether it is operable. VfIconButton has no inert-until-enhanced state, so unlike VfInput there is nothing here that either adapter may render differently.

dom.relationships.description: label[for], aria-describedby, aria-labelledby and aria-controls compared as a resolved relationship graph. Generated id values are canonicalised to their document position; the edges they create are not.

dom.wrapperPresence.description: Present so the comparator has a classification for it, and exact rather than framework-specific: a render-only button has no wrapper either adapter may add. If this ever produces a difference, something is wrong.

dom.inertAction.description: Present for the same reason as dom.wrapperPresence. VfIconButton renders no inert action, so a difference here is a defect, not a platform trait.

style.geometry.description: width, height, padding, border width and radius, font size, line height.

style.colour.description: colour, background colour and border colour, which is where token drift shows.

visual.description: Clipped screenshot of the case root in its initial state, per theme.

visual.postInteraction.description: Clipped screenshot of the case root after the interaction scenario has run, per theme. This is what makes an interaction case detect a change that leaves the DOM intact, such as content that is present but invisible.

a11y.role.description: Computed role of the control and of every action.

a11y.name.description: Accessible name of the control and of every action.

a11y.states.description: disabled, readonly, required and invalid as exposed to assistive tech.

interaction.focus.description: Which role owns focus after the scenario. Reported as a role rather than an element, because the adapters generate different ids and the question is whether the control got focus.

interaction.state.description: The post-scenario snapshot: the value, filled on the field and on the control, floating, invalid, disabled, readonly, operability and the control class list.

interaction.value.description: Present for the shared comparator. A button carries no value, so this never produces a difference.

interaction.selection.description: Present for the shared comparator. A button carries no caret, so this never produces a difference.

interaction.wrapperPresence.description: Present for the shared comparator. VfIconButton renders no wrapper that could appear on one side only.

interaction.relationships.description: Whether the label still reaches this control after the scenario, and what each aria-describedby token resolves to.

historicalQuirks.description: v-bind="attrs" is written after the component’s own bindings, so a consumer attribute overrides them. An explicit aria-invalid="false" survives an invalid control. VfButton does the opposite.
historicalQuirks.reason: Both adapters reproduce it: the Razor component only computes aria-invalid when the caller did not supply one. Recorded because two form controls in the same library have opposite precedence.

historicalQuirks.description: The filled test is string length rather than trimmed content, so three spaces count as filled and a floating label lifts over them.
historicalQuirks.reason: Shared with VfInput, which is why both adapters call the same isInputFilled rule rather than restating it.

historicalQuirks.description: The control reads the field placement rather than whether the field actually floated, so a floating-placement field with no label still marks the control.
historicalQuirks.reason: Identical to VfInput. Reproduced rather than tidied.

historicalQuirks.description: There is no rows prop. The row count is a native attribute a consumer forwards, so the component never sets a default height of its own.
historicalQuirks.reason: Recorded because a port would reasonably expect a rows prop on a textarea component and inventing one would be new product surface.
